newsitem.title: USA: Ali wows crowd, takes another jab at Frazier.
newsitem.headline: Ali wows crowd, takes another jab at Frazier.

text.p: Boxing legend Muhammad Ali brought his campaign of racial and religious tolerance to the nation's capital on Monday, showing he is still a great crowd-pleaser, no matter how frail and unintelligible.

Ali, 55, spoke few words because of the Parkinson's Syndrome disease from which he suffers, but nonetheless electrified the audience of about 1,000 at George Washington University with periodic gestures, facial expressions, or brief quips.

At the same time, Ali couldn't resist taking yet another jab at old nemesis Joe Frazier, joking that "Joe Frazier can't read," no doubt opening an old wound. Frazier has considered Ali's jokes an insulting and racially insensitive portrayal of an uneducated African American.

Here to promote a book, "Healing - A Journal of Tolerance and Understanding," on which he collaborated with author and longtime friend Thomas Hauser, Ali called several admirers to the stage, granting them wishes of being close to the champ.

"Twenty-three years ago, I came to this country with the dream of meeting Muhammad Ali," Hossein Shieky, a native of Iran, said during a question-and-answer session. "This is not an exaggeration. I just drove 80 mph (130 kph) to get here."
Ali, who converted to Islam in 1964, called him to the stage with a wave of the hand, and the two exchanged hugs and kisses on the cheek.

Another man, Orkendell Ford, said he was a schoolmate of Ali's back in Louisville, Kentucky, boxing with him as a youth in the 1960s. He, too, was called to the stage for a mock round of fisticuffs, and Ali's surprisingly swift footwork drew howls of approval from the crowd.
Ali's comment about Frazier also got a laugh. It came when he was asked by an audience member whether Frazier had read "Healing" in an effort to repair their torn relationship.

Frazier has publicly and repeatedly expressed malevolence for Ali, one of the world's best-loved figures, for what he considered Ali's degrading and insulting remarks about Frazier during and after their three great title fights of the 1970s.
That dates to Ali's reference to his fellow African American fighter as a "gorilla" in the promotion of their famous "Thrilla in Manila" fight.
Ali's wife, Lonnie Ali, who served as his interpreter on stage, was quick to point out that the remark about Frazier was "in jest."
